questions.text: A chemical company operates a production plant that emits CO2 directly, purchases electricity and sells chemicals that customers later process. Which emissions classification is consistent with the GHG framework?

options.a: Plant emissions are Scope 1 and purchased electricity is Scope 2, but downstream customer processing is excluded from every Scope 3 inventory.
options.b: Plant emissions are Scope 1; electricity is Scope 3; customer use is Scope 2.
options.c: Plant emissions are Scope 3; electricity is Scope 2; customer use is Scope 1.
options.d: Plant emissions are Scope 1; electricity is Scope 2; customer use is Scope 3.
options.e: Plant emissions are Scope 2; electricity is Scope 1; customer use is Scope 3.
options.f: Plant emissions are Scope 2; purchased energy is Scope 3; customer processing is outside all three scopes.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Impact materiality asks how the enterprise affects people or the environment.
II. Financial materiality asks how sustainability matters affect enterprise cash flows or financing.
III. Under double materiality, a topic must be material from both perspectives to be reportable.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and II only
options.b: III only
options.c: I and III only
options.d: II and III only
options.f: None of I, II or III

questions.text: A manufacturer faces flood risks that threaten future production, while its wastewater also harms a nearby ecosystem without an identified immediate financial cost. Under ESRS double materiality, which assessment is appropriate?

options.a: Only the wastewater is potentially material because ESRS excludes financial risk to operations.
options.b: Neither issue can be reported until both have separately caused recognized accounting losses.
options.c: Both exposures require an already recognized IAS 37 loss provision before they can feature in an ESRS materiality assessment.
options.d: Only the flood risk is potentially material because ESRS considers investor cash flows exclusively.
options.e: Flood risk may be financially material and wastewater may be impact-material, either of which can trigger reporting.

questions.text: The lecture contrasts IFRS S1/S2 and GRI reporting. Which distinction is most consistent with that comparison?

options.a: IFRS S1/S2 centers on ecological impact only; GRI emphasizes equity valuation from investors.
options.b: Both require reporting only after an environmental impact creates recognized accounting losses.
options.c: GRI focuses only on changes in a firm’s financing cost, while IFRS S1/S2 reports only impacts on external stakeholders.
options.d: GRI requires a quantified market value for every ecological impact before any disclosure can be issued.
options.e: Both are simply alternative names for the IFRS consolidated income statement and balance sheet.
options.f: IFRS S1/S2 centers on investor-relevant financial materiality; GRI emphasizes impacts on stakeholders.

questions.text: A firm's Scope 1 emissions are 20,000 tCO2e, Scope 2 are 10,000 and Scope 3 are 70,000. Its Scope 3 share of the full inventory is:
A company generates €500m in annual sales, Scope 1 emissions of 48,000 tCO2e and Scope 2 of 12,000 tCO2e. Its Scope 1+2 carbon intensity is:

options.a: 150 tCO2e per €m of sales.
options.b: 120 tCO2e per €m of sales.
options.c: 600 tCO2e per €m of sales.
options.d: 96 tCO2e per €m of sales.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. The greenhouse-gas reporting boundary must always coincide exactly with the IFRS consolidation boundary.
II. Scope 3 often involves estimates across suppliers and customers.
III. Scope 2 can be presented using both location-based and market-based estimates.
Which set is correct?

options.a: II and III only
options.b: None of I, II or III
options.c: I and III only
options.d: I, II and III

questions.text: A firm reports an 18% reduction in Scope 2 market-based emissions but unchanged location-based emissions. Which explanation is most plausible?

options.a: A reduction in the physical emissions of all grid generators serving its operating regions.
options.b: Changes in electricity procurement or certificate claims, without lower grid-average emissions exposure.
options.c: Market-based and location-based Scope 2 must change by identical percentages, because both rely exclusively on average grid factors.
options.d: A reduction in Scope 1 fuel combustion recorded in a separately owned production facility.
options.e: Location-based emissions are recalculated only after a company receives an unmodified external audit opinion.
options.f: An elimination of all upstream and downstream emissions regardless of purchased electricity.

questions.text: Company A reduces absolute Scope 1+2 emissions by 5% while revenue falls by 20%. Ignoring measurement changes, what happens to its emissions intensity per euro of sales?

options.a: It increases by 18.75% despite the fall in absolute emissions.
options.b: It decreases by exactly 5%, matching the change in emissions.
options.c: It increases by exactly 20%, matching the revenue contraction.
options.d: It decreases by 18.75% because absolute emissions have fallen.
options.e: It increases by about 15% because reduced revenue outweighs the lower emissions.

questions.text: A company's emissions rise from 80,000 to 92,000 tCO2e, while turnover increases from €400m to €500m. Which assessment is consistent with the two measures?

options.a: Absolute emissions decline 25%, while emissions intensity remains fixed at 184 tCO2e/€m.
options.b: Absolute emissions rise 12%, while intensity falls to 160 tCO2e/€m of sales.
options.c: Absolute emissions decline 15%, but emissions intensity rises from 184 to 200 tCO2e/€m.
options.d: Absolute emissions rise 15%, but emissions intensity declines from 200 to 184 tCO2e/€m.
options.e: Absolute emissions rise 25%, while emissions intensity remains fixed at 200 tCO2e/€m.
options.f: Absolute emissions rise 15%, and therefore carbon intensity must rise 15% even if turnover increases faster.

questions.text: A multinational includes acquired subsidiaries in its financial consolidation but excludes them from its published carbon inventory. What should an analyst investigate?

options.a: Whether the subsidiaries were fully eliminated from the firm's reported consolidated equity.
options.b: Whether Scope 3 must always equal the value of the acquired goodwill in tCO2e.
options.c: Differences in the emissions reporting boundary and their effect on comparability.
options.d: Whether cash-flow classification rules prohibit all acquisitions by emissions reporters.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Falling carbon intensity alone proves that absolute emissions have also declined.
II. A renewable-energy share relates renewable energy consumed to total energy consumed.
III. A green-capex share can compare taxonomy-aligned capital spending with total capex.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and II only
options.b: I and III only
options.c: III only
options.d: II and III only

questions.text: A company spends €90m of its €600m annual capital expenditures on taxonomy-aligned investment. Its green-capex share is:
A firm has 120 employees leave during the year and an average headcount of 1,500. Its employee turnover ratio is:
Two plants have 18 and 12 recordable work accidents respectively. Plant A works 3m hours; Plant B works 1.5m hours. Which has the higher accident rate per million hours?

options.a: Plant B: 8 per million hours, versus Plant A: 6.
options.b: Plant A: 6 per million hours, versus Plant B: 4.
options.c: Plant A: 6 per million hours, versus Plant B: 8, so A has the higher normalized accident rate.
options.d: Plant B: 12 per million hours, versus Plant A: 6.
options.e: Plant A: 12 per million hours, versus Plant B: 8.

questions.text: A company reports average male pay of €60,000 and female pay of €51,000. Using the lecture's gender-pay-gap formula, the result is:

Consider the statements.
I. An ESG-linked-pay ratio compares relevant variable remuneration with total variable pay.
II. An employee turnover ratio is independent of workforce size by definition.
III. A board independence ratio measures independent directors relative to total board size.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and II only
options.b: None of I, II or III
options.c: III only
options.d: I, II and III

questions.text: An auditor concludes that one material inventory balance is misstated, but the problem is not pervasive throughout the statements. Which report is most consistent with that finding?

options.a: Unmodified opinion
options.b: Disclaimer of opinion
options.c: A disclaimer, because an isolated material misstatement prevents the auditor from obtaining enough evidence.
options.d: Adverse opinion

questions.text: An auditor finds material and pervasive misstatements across several accounts and has sufficient evidence to reach that conclusion. Which audit opinion is appropriate?

options.a: Unmodified opinion
options.b: Disclaimer of opinion
options.c: Qualified opinion
options.d: A qualified opinion, because sufficient evidence eliminates any possibility of pervasive misstatement.
options.e: An adverse opinion is inappropriate until creditors have experienced a cash loss from the misstatements.

questions.text: An auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about a pervasive portion of the financial statements. What is the appropriate reporting outcome?

options.a: A qualified opinion only, because an audit report cannot disclaim a conclusion on the financial statements.
options.b: Unmodified opinion
options.c: Disclaimer of opinion
options.d: An adverse opinion even though the problem concerns missing evidence rather than identified pervasive misstatements.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. A key audit matter identifies an area of significant audit attention and judgment.
II. An unmodified opinion does not guarantee that no future fraud will be discovered.
III. Any key audit matter automatically converts an unmodified opinion into an adverse one.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and II only
options.b: I, II and III
options.c: III only
options.d: II and III only

questions.text: A listed firm's audit report highlights goodwill impairment as a KAM but expresses an unmodified opinion. Which conclusion is warranted?

options.a: The auditor declined to express an opinion because it discussed future cash-flow forecasts.
options.b: The valuation relied on significant judgment, but the KAM itself does not modify the audit opinion.
options.c: The goodwill carrying amount is misstated because every KAM represents an adverse finding.
options.d: The company must reverse all recognized goodwill because it received an unmodified opinion.

questions.text: A company reported three KAMs last year and four this year, including a new revenue-recognition issue. What is the most informative analytical approach?

options.a: Ignore the new KAM because an auditor is prohibited from discussing revenue recognition judgments.
options.b: Conclude that at least one additional fraud has occurred because the KAM count increased by one.
options.c: Investigate why a new issue required significant audit attention, rather than treating KAM count as proof of fraud.
options.d: Assume the audit opinion is now necessarily qualified because there are more than three KAMs.

questions.text: A firm pays €2m audit fees and reports €4bn in assets. Its audit fee intensity relative to assets is:

Consider the statements.
I. Delayed publication of audited results proves that all previously issued opinions were adverse.
II. A going-concern uncertainty flag concerns risks to continued operation.
III. An unmodified opinion can coexist with a going-concern uncertainty disclosure.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and II only
options.b: II only
options.c: None of I, II or III
options.d: II and III only

questions.text: A firm holds 400 issued patents, but 10 account for almost all licensing revenue. Why is total patent count a weak standalone valuation metric?

options.a: Patent value is skewed, and counts do not capture economic quality or citations.
options.b: Patent grants are all capitalized at their potential future revenue under IAS 38.
options.c: Patent counts are irrelevant because patents never create rights enforceable against rivals.
options.d: Patent count and fair market value must be identical for every firm under IFRS.

questions.text: Patent applications jump from 120 last year to 150 this year. Using a conventional growth-rate calculation, the increase is:
A technology company has 60 patent grants on €300m R&D expense; a competitor has 45 grants on €150m R&D. Which has the greater patent grants per €m of R&D?

options.a: The competitor: 0.30 versus 0.20 grants/€m.
options.b: The first firm: 0.20 versus 0.15 grants/€m.
options.c: The competitor: 0.15 grants/€m compared with 0.20 for the first firm.
options.d: Both firms: 0.20 grants/€m after normalization.
options.f: The first firm: 0.30 grants/€m compared with 0.20 for the competitor.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Strategic patent filings can aim to block competitors instead of only marketing new products.
II. European patent applications are commonly published before the patents are granted.
III. Most internally developed patent value is fully recognized as an IFRS asset at market value.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I, II and III
options.b: II only
options.c: I and II only
options.d: I and III only

questions.text: A firm files significantly fewer patents than a rival but relies heavily on proprietary production secrets. Which inference is most defensible?

options.a: Lower patent counts necessarily imply fewer productive inventions and lower future operating income.
options.b: Under IFRS, trade secrets are always recorded at a higher valuation than patents are.
options.c: Trade secrets must be disclosed publicly before their economic benefit can be recognized.
options.d: Lower patent counts may reflect a different intellectual-property strategy rather than lower innovation.

questions.text: An analyst wants to assess a newly announced patent portfolio before annual financial statements are released. Which information would add the most insight beyond simple filing counts?

options.a: Forward citations, technological relevance and whether major inventions are commercially used.
options.b: The nominal value of outstanding share capital and the next coupon payment date.
options.c: Total dividends paid in the year regardless of invention disclosures or field differences.
options.d: Average employee age with no regard to the firm's sector or patent citation patterns.

questions.text: A biotech company has 12 pipeline candidates: two in Phase III, one filed for approval and nine in earlier stages. Its late-stage pipeline share is:
A firm has ten development projects, seven aimed at the same lead indication. What does the pipeline-concentration ratio signal?

options.a: 30% of candidate drugs have reached Phase III or formal filing for approval.
options.b: 70% of candidate drugs have received regulatory approval for commercial sale.
options.c: 70% reliance on one indication, creating concentrated scientific or regulatory exposure.
options.d: 30% reliance on one indication, creating diversified scientific or regulatory exposure.

questions.text: A biotech has €180m cash and cash equivalents and uses €60m cash annually in operations, at a stable rate. Ignoring investment spending, roughly how much operating cash runway remains?

options.a: 3 years
options.b: 6 years
options.c: 3.5 years
options.d: 2 years

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Phase I trials focus mainly on initial safety assessment.
II. Most drugs entering Phase I are ultimately approved for sale.
III. Phase III trials are generally larger confirmatory studies.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and III only
options.b: III only
options.c: II and III only
options.d: I and II only

questions.text: A small biotech announces failure of its only late-stage drug trial. Why can this produce an unusually large share-price reaction even if the drug had no recognized balance-sheet value?

options.a: IAS 38 guarantees that all failed products were previously recognized at their final sales value.
options.b: The firm cannot lose market value due to a failed trial if its internally generated R&D was expensed rather than capitalized.
options.c: Failed trials must automatically generate cash inflows equal to the original drug-development spending.
options.d: The failure has no valuation effect because the expected product did not appear as an IFRS intangible.
options.e: Expected future cash flows may collapse despite much internal R&D being expensed rather than capitalized.

questions.text: A pharmaceutical group buys a drug candidate in an acquisition; a separate group develops a similar candidate entirely internally. Which accounting difference is most plausible?

options.a: Neither candidate can be recognized as an intangible asset until its commercial launch date.
options.b: Both candidates automatically create goodwill equal to the combined future forecast revenue.
options.c: Acquired in-process R&D may be recognized at fair value; most internal research is expensed.
options.d: Acquired in-process R&D must be expensed; most internally developed research is fair-valued.

questions.text: A product candidate recorded as an acquired intangible subsequently fails a pivotal trial. What should an analyst particularly expect management to evaluate?

options.a: Reclassification of the drug candidate as a cash equivalent pending a new study.
options.b: Management must keep the acquired candidate at historical acquisition cost even after definitive failure of the pivotal trial.
options.c: The intangible becomes an inventory asset immediately because its commercial approval is now delayed.
options.d: Reversal of all prior research costs into the new current-period revenue line.
options.e: Impairment of the recognized candidate asset following the adverse development.
options.f: Recognition of a current financing cash receipt for the estimated failed trial cost.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Several executives purchasing shares together may strengthen an information signal.
II. All publicly reported insider trades necessarily involve illegal use of inside information.
III. An insider purchase can be more informative than a sale motivated by liquidity needs.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and III only
options.b: I and II only
options.c: I, II and III
options.d: II and III only

questions.text: A chief executive buys a substantial stake with personal funds, while three other directors buy similar positions. Another executive sells a small holding under a pre-planned program. Which signal deserves the closest follow-up?

options.a: The preplanned transaction necessarily conveys stronger information because insider sales always predict price declines.
options.b: The absence of a share-price change because manager trades have no information content.
options.c: A scheduled insider disposal always conveys a stronger positive signal than discretionary executive purchases, because it was arranged in advance.
options.d: The cluster of sizeable discretionary purchases rather than the routine scheduled sale.
options.e: The total salary expense because insider purchases are a contractual source of revenue.
options.f: The small pre-planned sale because every sale reflects expected company-wide losses.

questions.text: Under the lecture's EU managers' transactions framework, which statement correctly distinguishes lawful disclosure from prohibited insider dealing?

options.a: A disclosed trade is automatically illegal if it occurs outside the annual closed period.
options.b: A disclosed lawful trade does not authorize dealing on material non-public inside information.
options.c: Disclosure makes any trade lawful, even when it is based on undisclosed price-sensitive facts.
options.d: Illegal insider dealing is restricted to transactions in the employer's own ordinary shares.

questions.text: According to the lecture's November 2026 discussion of EU MAR, the standard notification threshold since December 2024 is €20,000 per calendar year. Which additional qualification matters?

options.a: National regulators may apply a threshold from €10,000 to €50,000.
options.b: Notifications are required only after a calendar year's final annual report.
options.c: The same €20,000 threshold applies uniformly to all EU member states and cannot be altered by national regulators.
options.d: The threshold applies only to cash dividends, not securities transactions.
options.e: Every EU market must apply a fixed €5,000 threshold without any variation.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Managers must report every trade before execution to obtain a public audit opinion.
II. PDMR transaction notifications generally have a three-business-day deadline in the lecture.
III. A closed period restricts managers' dealings before scheduled interim or annual results.
Which set is correct?

options.a: I and III only
options.b: None of I, II or III
options.c: I, II and III
options.d: II and III only

questions.text: A finance executive learns confidential acquisition news about Firm A and purchases shares in publicly traded supplier Firm B because it is expected to benefit. This is an example of:

options.a: a lawful disclosure of audit key matters by the auditor.
options.b: shadow trading in an economically linked firm.
options.c: a normal patent cross-licensing arrangement.
options.d: routine treasury share repurchases by the issuer.

questions.text: A manager has no reported trades in the employing firm, but market surveillance identifies unusual options trading in a peer just before a takeover announcement. What principle makes this potentially relevant?

options.a: Inside information can have value for economically linked issuers beyond the employer itself.
options.b: A peer firm's options are classified as goodwill of the original employer.
options.c: Only transactions in the employer's own shares can exploit confidential information.
options.d: Trade information is irrelevant until the companies' financial year ends.

questions.text: Which limitation most directly undermines treating a single insider sale as proof that the company's outlook is poor?

options.a: Every insider sale mechanically increases the issuer's retained earnings account.
options.b: Sales may reflect diversification, taxes or personal liquidity rather than adverse expectations.
options.c: A single insider sale always changes the firm's operating cash flow by its sale amount.
options.d: All insider sales are required by EU law to occur exactly 30 days before results.

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Every ESG disclosure is measured with less estimation than audited financial statements.
II. Patent statistics can add information that internally generated intangible assets omit.
III. A clean audit opinion does not substitute for reviewing significant KAMs and forecasts.
Which set is correct?

options.a: II only
options.b: II and III only
options.c: I and III only
options.d: I, II and III

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. A KAM automatically means the auditor has issued an adverse opinion.
II. Scope 3 consists entirely of the firm's directly owned factory emissions.
III. Patent citation data can supplement crude patent-count statistics.
Which set is correct?

options.a: None of I, II or III
options.b: I only
options.c: II and III only
options.d: II only

questions.text:
Consider the statements.
I. Insider sales may reflect diversification rather than pessimistic expectations.
II. A clinical trial failure can change a biotech's intrinsic value.
III. An unmodified audit opinion can coexist with identified KAMs.
Which set is correct?

options.a: III only
options.b: I and III only
options.c: I, II and III
options.d: I and II only
